analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance program covering every U.S. resident with no deductibles or copays.
analysis.headline: A single-payer health bill with 78 cosponsors — including Nancy Pelosi and Chuck Schumer — was referred to five committees in March 1991 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, federal employees' insurance, military and veterans' health coverage with one national health insurance program for every U.S. citizen and lawful resident. It would cover hospital care, doctors, prescription drugs, mental health care, nursing home and home care with no copays or deductibles. Providers would be paid from a national trust fund financed by higher income taxes, an uncapped hospital insurance payroll tax, and a monthly premium for seniors above low incomes. It was referred to five House committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed comprehensive coverage with no out-of-pocket cost at the point of care — the uninsured, people whose insurance has gaps or high deductibles, Medicare beneficiaries who pay premiums and coinsurance, and families paying private insurance premiums. Hospitals would gain a guaranteed paying customer for every patient, ending uncompensated care for the uninsured.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents needing health care

how_it_helps.text: Every citizen, national, and lawful resident alien is entitled to comprehensive health benefits, enrolled automatically at birth or immigration [S3].

Covered services include hospital care, nursing facility and home health services, hospice, physician and professional services, prescription drugs, and preventive care, with no coinsurance, deductibles, or copayments [S2, S3].
Providers must accept the program's payment as payment in full, so patients would owe nothing beyond their taxes [S2, S3].
Mental health care is covered, though capped at 45 inpatient days and 20 outpatient visits per year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income households and corporations bear the largest costs: the top corporate rate rises from 34% to 38%, and individual rates jump to 30% starting just above roughly $19,450 of taxable income (single filer), reaching 38% over $120,000 [S3]. All workers and employers pay higher hospital insurance payroll taxes, with no cap on the wages subject to them, and up to 85% of Social Security benefits become taxable [S2, S3]. Seniors above low incomes pay a $55 monthly premium, collected from Social Security checks [S2, S3]. States must make annual maintenance-of-effort payments into the fund [S3].

drawbacks.text: The financing is broad, not only progressive: the bill creates a new 30% income tax bracket beginning just above $19,450 of taxable income for single filers, raises the employer hospital insurance tax to 7.5% with no wage cap, and taxes 85% of Social Security benefits [S3].
Seniors with incomes above roughly $8,500 ($10,700 joint) pay a new $55 monthly long-term care/health care premium, deducted from Social Security checks [S3].
Mental health benefits are limited to 45 inpatient days and 20 outpatient psychotherapy visits per year, less generous than many private plans of the era [S3].

Every provider must accept the program's fee schedule or global budget as payment in full, eliminating balance billing and giving the Secretary and review commissions substantial power over provider revenue [S2, S3].

The bill terminates Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, CHAMPUS, and veterans' health benefits on a single date (December 31, 1994), making the transition to the new program high-stakes with no fallback if the new system faltered [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage gain is enormous and universal — no copays, deductibles, or premiums for most people, and no one uninsured. The cost is real and broadly shared: tax increases reaching well into middle incomes, an uncapped payroll tax on employers, and a new senior premium, all feeding a national health budget that grows only with the gross national product, which could tighten payments to providers over time. The all-at-once termination of five existing federal health programs adds transition risk. Weighing it honestly: a major expansion for ordinary people paid for by a large, partly regressive tax increase on workers and employers, and by the elimination of the private-role in basic coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees and three subcommittees in March 1991, gathered 78 cosponsors over the next year and a half, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Russo of Illinois introduced the bill on March 6, 1991, joined as original cosponsors by 21 other House members including Nancy Pelosi, Chuck Schumer, Charles Rangel, John Dingell-era liberals Marty Russo ally Joseph Moody, Ed Markey, and others [S3].
The bill was referred jointly to five committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Post Office and Civil Service, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs [S3, S5].

Within three weeks it was sent to subcommittees — Military Personnel and Compensation, Health, Compensation and Employee Benefits, and Health and the Environment — and no committee or subcommittee ever took recorded action beyond that referral [S5].
Sponsors kept adding cosponsors through September 1992, reaching 78 total — 77 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
The 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, with the bill never reported out of committee and never voted on in either chamber [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance industry and the existing multi-payer system — private insurers, and providers and employers invested in the current payment structure — were better off, since the bill that would have replaced it with a single government program never came to a vote. Members of Congress were also spared a vote on a bill that would have raised taxes broadly while eliminating Medicare, Medicaid, and employer-based federal coverage in one step.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo system

sides.party_line_note: All 77 Democratic cosponsors outnumbered a single Republican; no committee chaired under the Democratic majority ever brought the bill to a vote.

industries.note: The bill terminates Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, CHAMPUS, and veterans' coverage and replaces them with a single public program whose claims would be processed by one competitively bid fiscal agent per state, largely displacing private insurers. Insurers' revenue depended on the fragmented multi-payer system the bill abolished.

Hospitals would be paid through annual global budgets approved by state advisory boards and the Secretary instead of per-service billing, and could charge patients nothing beyond program payment. They would gain universal coverage eliminating uncompensated care, but lose the ability to bill insurers and patients above the budget.

Doctors would be paid on a Secretary-set fee schedule and must accept it as payment in full, but would gain a guaranteed paying patient for every visit and no bad debt or collections. Their trade of billing freedom for guaranteed payment put them at odds with parts of the bill and aligned with others.
Prescription drugs would be covered for everyone with no cost-sharing, expanding the customer base, but payment would run through fee schedules set within a capped national budget.

The top corporate tax rate rises from 34% to 38%, and new 30-38% income tax brackets reach down to roughly $19,450 in taxable income for single filers, with Social Security benefits taxed at up to 85%.
